Our method learns an in-context score operator that maps the context samples, a noisy query point, and the diffusion time to the task-dependent score, enabling reverse-diffusion sampling on unseen tasks without retraining or parameter updates. A key observation is that the task-dependent score admits a Gaussian-kernel conditional-mean representation. Its empirical Nadaraya--Watson approximation can be represented exactly by a model in our constructed transformer class, providing a principled foundation for the proposed query-dependent attention architecture. The operator is trained through amortized denoising score matching across task distributions. We establish generalization-error bounds that quantify the effects of the context size, the numbers of training tasks and within-task samples, model complexity, and intrinsic and ambient dimensions. Numerically, we evaluate the method on a range of scientific and visual datasets, including Navier-Stokes, ERA5 climate data, QuickDraw sketches, and Food-101. The results show that the proposed method performs well on relatively simple task families, while its performance degrades as task complexity increases, thereby illustrating both the promise and the limitations of in-context learning for diffusion models.

title: On a conjecture on Romanoff type representations
abstract: Let $r_1,\ldots,r_t$ be positive integers, and let $\mathcal A$ be the set of integers of the form $2^{k_1^{r_1}}+\cdots+2^{k_t^{r_t}}$, where $k_1,\ldots,k_t$ are positive integers. For any positive integer $n$, let $r(n)$ be the number of representations $n=p+a$ with $p$ an odd prime and $a\in \mathcal A$. We prove that if $r_1^{-1}+\cdots+r_t^{-1}=1$, then, for every fixed positive integer $m$, the set of integers $n$ with $r(n)\ge m$ has positive lower asymptotic density. In particular, this confirms a conjecture of Chen.

title: Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient is Nearly Minimax-Optimal
abstract: Standard Policy Gradient (PG) algorithms suffer from high estimation variance because they rely on Monte Carlo updates. While off-policy variance reduction mitigates this problem, establishing optimal sample complexity currently requires either restrictive assumptions, such as uniformly bounded importance weights, or impractical second-order operations. In this work, we introduce Loopless Variance-Reduced PG (LVR-PG), a unified theoretical framework that abstracts a class of first-order estimators that integrate recursive updates with defensive importance sampling, including known estimators such as PAGE-PG and STORM-PG. We prove that this algorithmic class achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(ε^{-2})$ last-iterate global convergence under weak gradient domination for general parametric policies. We establish this guarantee using purely first-order updates, with minimal assumptions and without gradient preconditioners. By extending state-of-the-art lower bounds to continuous parametric policies, we establish an $Ω(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity limit, confirming our framework is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.

title: Calibration in One Go: Jointly Learning Accurate and Calibrated Neural Networks
abstract: Neural networks (NNs), while highly flexible and versatile, are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration methods adjust the outputs of an already trained model using a separate calibration dataset and additional calibration parameters. This process adds overhead that requires separate optimization of the calibrator and subsequent model selection. In this paper, we show that standard (post-hoc) calibrators can be trained end-to-end with the backbone via a bilevel Stackelberg formulation. This formulation eliminates the need for a separate calibration set or a dedicated calibration loss by jointly optimizing accuracy and calibration using cross-entropy, introducing only one additional hyperparameter: the calibrator learning rate. Although our framework supports calibrators ranging from temperature and matrix scaling to NN layers, our results show that using the final classification layer itself as the calibrator yields accurate, well-calibrated models with no additional parameters. Our approach outperforms SOTA calibrators with minimal added complexity, while also avoiding the multiplicative overhead of separate calibration components in settings such as multi-task learning.

title: QTN-RQNN: Quantum Tensor Network-Based Recurrent Quantum Neural Network
abstract: Resource constraints and imperfect quantum operations remain major challenges for quantum machine learning (QML) on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, particularly for fault-diagnosis tasks involving imbalanced and heterogeneous data. This work proposes QTN-RQNN, a Quantum Tensor Network-Based Recurrent Quantum Neural Network that integrates tensor-network-inspired nearest-neighbor interactions with recurrent quantum processing. The model sequentially encodes input features while propagating quantum memory across recurrent steps and incorporates QSMOTE for class balancing. QTN-RQNN is evaluated on four heterogeneous fault-diagnosis datasets SPID, CWRUBD, EFDD, and SFDD and compared with QNN, QTN-QNN, and RQNN baselines through classification, ablation, multi-seed, convergence, and quantum-resource analyses. Results show dataset-dependent predictive behavior, indicating that increased quantum architectural complexity does not universally improve classification. On SPID, QTN-RQNN improves the RQNN F1-score from 0.3077 to 0.4516 and ROC-AUC from 0.4485 to 0.6970, while the remaining datasets exhibit different performance-resource trade-offs and sensitivity to recurrent timesteps and circuit depth. Across all datasets, QTN-RQNN reduces the two-qubit-gate count from 32 to 24 per sample relative to RQNN, corresponding to a 25% reduction without increasing the four-qubit requirement; the same relative reduction is obtained for QTN-QNN over QNN. These findings establish QTN-RQNN as a resource-conscious recurrent quantum architecture and highlight the need to jointly consider predictive performance and circuit-resource requirements for near-term quantum fault diagnosis.

title: Verifiable Retrieval for Legal Reasoning through Structure-driven Knowledge Graph
abstract: Any automation within reliability-critical contexts such as medicine or law has to be transparent and verifiable. Despite their advantages, current LLM-based systems do not meet these requirements due to their inherent black-box nature. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) attempts to ground the generative process in the relevant interpretable documents, thereby reducing the risk of AI 'hallucinations' and potentially enabling verification of the initial generation context. However, as the number and size of potential sources increases, naive retrieval approaches tend to perform worse, ignoring critical context elements. In this paper we aim to tackle this problem in the context of German Legal Code. Using structure-driven parsing to create a Knowledge Graph (KG) for the source document navigation and retrieval, we compare several KG-informed chunking and retrieval strategies and evaluate their effect on the accuracy of retrieved citations.

title: Differences among preparatory processes preceding major earthquakes in Kamchatka, 2014-2025, including the MW 8.8 event
abstract: Earthquake preparation involves progressive damage accumulation, strain localization, and changes in the organization of seismicity. We investigate preparatory processes preceding seven episodes of major earthquakes in the Kuril - Kamchatka subduction zone during 2014 - 2025, including the 29 July 2025 MW 8.8 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake. We track damage evolution using the seismic regularity coefficient dc and seismic strain dynamics coefficient SSD, defined for seismic series. Before 2022, each episode of strong seismicity was preceded by a pronounced dc minimum, commonly accompanied by an SSD minimum, followed by an increase in dc toward a maximum near the strong event or event group. After 2022, dc minima became shallower and were superimposed on a sustained upward trend. We interpret this transition as evidence that the metrics recorded two superimposed processes. The cycles before 2022 reflect complete strain-localization histories on southern or more distant structures that did not contribute to the segment ruptured in 2025. In contrast, the upward dc trend from 2022, with only shallow minima preceding Episodes 6 and 7, marks coupled behavior within the eventual main rupture segment, also influenced by stress transfer from southern source regions.

title: Improving Semantic Coverage in AI Test & Evaluation through Generative Augmentation
abstract: In test and evaluation (T&E) of AI models, evaluators typically have access only to a held-out test dataset and no knowledge of the training data or its semantic composition. If critical input conditions---such as time-of-day, weather, or scene location---are underrepresented in this test dataset, T&E results can be misleadingly due to this semantic coverage gap. We propose a three-stage generative AI pipeline to detect and fill such semantic gaps without requiring ground-truth labels of these semantics. First, vision-language models (VLMs) perform zero-shot binary labeling of semantic factors, and an embedding-space clustering step identifies which semantics most affect downstream model behavior. Second, diffusion-based image-to-image models transform existing covered images into the underrepresented semantic domain, preserving scene content while augmenting high-level appearance. Third, statistical analysis of the augmented image embeddings verifies that the synthetic imagery improves dataset coverage before it is incorporated. Crucially, the synthetic data is used only to enrich the test set and no model retraining is performed for T&E. We validate the full pipeline on both image classification and object detection under day/night semantic gaps, showing that the augmented test datasets better distinguish models with and without exposure to the missing semantic, thereby yielding T&E conclusions that more closely match those of an ideal, fully covered dataset. Code available at https://github.com/Hashe037/DEDUCE

title: DIA: A Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Interest-Aware ABR Scheme for Cloud Gaming
abstract: The continuous evolution of cloud gaming has enabled users to play high-quality cloud games on thin clients, such as smartphones and tablets. However, how to effectively transmit the gameplay frames with high resolution and low latency, especially over wireless networks, remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based Interest-Aware Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) scheme, called DIA, that guarantees the quality of perceptually key objects in each frame, while dynamically allocating lower resolutions for non-key objects to conserve bandwidth under constrained network conditions. By leveraging an off-the-shelf semantic segmentation model, the proposed DIA scheme can adjust the bitrate at the object-level. We also design a transformer-based feature extractor and an interest-aware reward function to enable the proposed DIA scheme to identify key objects and dynamically adjust their bitrates. This adaptation is guided by users' in-game movement speed, object features, and prevailing network conditions and operates without requiring additional hardware, such as gaze trackers. Extensive experiments show that the proposed DIA scheme outperforms existing ABR schemes in dynamic wireless network environments. Notably, DIA achieves at least a 20% higher normalized average Quality of Experience (QoE) than the State-Of-The-Art (SOTA) ABR algorithms in 5G scenarios.

title: The second type of power mean bounds for the hypergeometric mean
abstract: In this paper, by using signs rule for a class of special power series and for the Laplace integrals, we find the best power mean bounds for the hypergeometric function (sharp at the right endpoint). Our results contain many known conclusions.

title: Bessel-Hagen currents, reducibility charges, and local gravitational energy
abstract: We consider whether the translation Noether current of a linearised metric spin-2 theory admits a strictly gauge-invariant local representative. For Fierz-Pauli and dynamically regular pure curvature-squared theories in four dimensions, we show that no such representative exists under the stated locality, polynomiality and covariance assumptions. A direct enumeration first excludes nonzero symmetric rank-two tensors at the dimension and derivative order of the quadratic action: in the curvature-squared case, the parity-even conservation kernel consists of the identically vanishing Lanczos--Lovelock combination, while both parity-odd coefficients vanish. Homogeneity of the actions in total derivative number then allows projection by field degree and derivative number, extending the exclusion to all finite-order local polynomial representatives with constant coefficients and no explicit coordinate dependence. The translation current nevertheless defines a nonzero conserved-current class. Independently, a constant translation is a Killing reducibility parameter of the linearised gauge symmetry and determines a nonzero linear surface-charge class, which is distinct from the quadratic energy current. A separate calculation shows why a direct compensator cancellation available in Maxwell theory fails for the metric spin-2 field, although this calculation is not needed for the current-class result. Maxwell theory, propagating free $p$-forms and Yang--Mills theory linearised about the trivial vacuum provide comparisons in which translations are not reducibility parameters and strictly gauge-invariant stress tensors exist. Gauss--Bonnet and pure flat-space $R^2$ gravity lie outside the regular scope of the result, through variational triviality and dynamical degeneracy, respectively.

title: Optical atomic clocks on all-optical atom chips
abstract: The feasibility and potential performance of optical clocks based on all-optical atom chips using neutral strontium atoms have been investigated. The key benefits of all-optical atom chips are their ability to trap alkali-earth atoms, and how easily these atoms can be manipulated and examined. The planar configuration of the chip enables ring photonic resonators to be incorporated into its structure, making it a promising candidate for active optical atomic clocks. Using the 'magic wavelengths' of the trapping optical fields (813 nm and 390 nm for strontium atoms) minimises frequency shifts in the intercombination clock transition caused by variations in optical field intensity. However, this frequency shift can be compensated for using optical AC Stark shifts, which are generated by the trapping optical fields and have frequencies below the 'magic frequencies'. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that atom chip clocks can operate using solely repulsive, blue-detuned evanescent light fields when the attraction of the trapped atoms towards the photonic waveguide is realised through van der Waals forces alone. According to estimates, this could result in the short-term fractional frequency stability of the strontium atom-chip optical clocks being limited to ~10^{-16} per second, with an accuracy of about 5 x 10^{-15} for fractional intensity stability in the trapping light fields of 0.001.

title: Two-Sided Plausibility Constraints in Persuasion
abstract: A sender with commitment provides additional information to an already informed receiver. Final posterior means must be more dispersed than initial means and less dispersed than the state, in convex order. We characterize when these two plausibility constraints are also sufficient, so that every distribution satisfying them can be induced. If the state has a positive density, they are sufficient exactly under interval-partition information: the receiver learns which interval of a partition contains the state and nothing more, where an interval may be a single point. Otherwise, a nonempty open set of distributions satisfying both constraints cannot be induced, even when the sender observes the receiver's information. We use the sufficient case to derive an optimal symmetric disclosure rule in a second-price auction where bidders initially know valuation intervals.

title: A Baseline Assessment for the Agentic Web Technology Stack
abstract: The fast pace in which protocols, frameworks, and technologies are being proposed for LLM-based agents results in a complex scenario for anyone aiming to create state-of-the-art AI solutions. Without an assessment on how different protocols, frameworks, and libraries work together to compose an Agentic Web solution, developers and organizations face different challenges (e.g., skilling, governance, infrastructure) even before becoming part of the Agentic Web ecosystem. In this context, we propose a system for performing Agentic Web evaluations called MASTIF (Multi-Agent System TestIng Framework) and present a baseline assessment of Agentic Web technologies, including 3 LLMs, 3 protocols, and 4 agent implementation frameworks, against 300 Mind2Web benchmark tasks. Results suggest that selecting a task-specific technology stack may result in gains of task completion rate, efficiency score, and social value stability scores; and reductions in verbosity and time to complete tasks. With the presented results, we expect to present a baseline in terms of metrics and results for this complex and fast evolving scenario for those aiming at designing, assessing, and developing multi-agent systems.

title: Benchmarking Content-Defined Chunking Algorithms for Data Deduplication
abstract: Data deduplication relies on content-defined chunking (CDC) algorithms to decide where data is split. We observe that most CDC algorithms are modular: a base chunking algorithm fixes the byte-level cut-point condition, while high-level techniques (size normalization, min/max thresholds, caching) layer on top. Existing benchmarks conflate the two, obscuring which design choices actually drive performance. We isolate and evaluate eight state-of-the-art base chunking algorithms across four realistic workloads and four metrics: throughput, deduplication ratio, mean chunk size, and chunk-size variance. Further, we derive new formulas relating algorithm parameters to expected chunk size for AE, RAM, and MII. In doing so, we uncover a longstanding error in the widely-used AE parameterization reproduced across multiple papers and evaluation tools that produces chunks 13-39% smaller than intended and inflates AE's reported deduplication. Across our evaluation, AE is the most balanced base chunking algorithm across all four metrics, RAM's similarity to AE does not carry over to low-entropy data, and MII and PCI show limited advantages over simpler alternatives in storage-oriented workloads. We release all implementations, datasets, and analysis scripts as open source.

title: Critical Ising model as the $M(4,3)$ minimal model of conformal field theory
abstract: We construct a linear map from the space of spin polynomials in the critical Ising model on a lattice to the state space of the $M(4,3)$ minimal model of conformal field theory. The kernel of the map consists precisely of null fields, i.e., spin polynomials that vanish in all correlations. For a polynomial $\Op$ which is not a null field, we define its scaling dimension $Δ_{\Op}\in\Z_{\geq0}\cup(\Z_{\geq0}+\frac{1}{8}),$ to be the lowest $\Loper{0}+\Loperbar{0}$ eigenvalue in the decomposition of its image into homogeneous components. We show that as the mesh size $δ$ goes to zero, the rescaled field $δ^{-Δ_{\Op}}\Op$ has a non-trivial scaling limit, when inserted in correlations with other such fields. Moreover, all these limits can be expressed in terms of correlations of primary fields of $M(4,3)$ and the Virasoro action in the continuum. The highest weight vectors of $M(4,3)$, the joint eigenvectors of $\Loper{0}$ and $\Loperbar{0}$ with the same eigenvalues $0,1/16,1/2$ for both, are the images of the constant $1$, the spin at a single lattice vertex, and the energy at a single lattice edge, respectively. For the proof, we construct a map from a larger lattice field space, accommodating also fermion and disorder insertions, to a direct sum of two fermionic Fock spaces. This direct sum contains contains the state spaces of both the $M(4,3)$ and the free fermion CFT. The main technical ingredient of the proof is a new version of the exact fermionic current action on the space of lattice local fields due to C. Hongler, K.K. and F. Viklund, combined with some new advances in discrete complex analysis. Our results are valid on arbitrary isoradial graphs.

title: GLIMPSE: Global-Local Indexing with Multi-Precision Spectral Encoding for Explorable Video World Models
abstract: A camera-controlled video world model must keep a scene consistent when the camera returns to it. Memories that render stored features into the target frame can turn depth and pose errors into ghosting or duplicated structure. Positional transport avoids that resampling by relocating a historical patch's address rather than its content, but assigns full positional precision even to inaccurate projections. We present GLIMPSE, a global-local memory interface with band-wise multi-precision coordinates and geometry-conditioned spectral attenuation to reduce sensitivity to inaccurate projected addresses. Local patch memory supplies view-specific appearance, while recurrent global memory provides scene context. Footprint-guided retrieval selects historical patches under a fixed local read budget. Under matched retrieval and read budgets, GLIMPSE improves geometric correspondence and photometric consistency over deterministic positional transport.

title: A 9-dimensional nilpotent Lie algebra isomorphic to its complex conjugate admitting no real form
abstract: We give an explicit example of a 9-dimensional 5-step nilpotent complex Lie algebra, generated by two elements, that is isomorphic to its complex conjugate but has no real form. In contrast to the earlier 10-dimensional examples, our proof is completely elementary and very short.

title: Adaptive DHiSparse: Speculative Decoding over a Load-Adaptive KV Hierarchy
abstract: Long-context serving runs out of KV memory before the hardware reaches its useful throughput. HiSparse stores history in host memory and fetches only the selected entries, but it uses one cache budget at every load and does not handle draft-model speculative decoding such as DSpark and DFlash2. We present Adaptive DHiSparse, which supports speculative decoding over hierarchical sparse KV and adapts residency to load. It protects the required working set, retains additional history while GPU memory is spare, and recovers the rest through exact fused retrieval. DSpark and DFlash2 keep their proposal and acceptance rules: queries share missing-row retrieval, draft KV uses a window-bounded ring, and verification staging is reused across layer groups. At 100K context and concurrency 128, GLM-5.3 with DFlash2 delivers 793 output tokens/s per decode GPU, 1.45$\times$ HiSparse and 1.27$\times$ non-speculative adaptive serving. Held to the same latency bounds as HiSparse, it sustains up to 4$\times$ the concurrency and 2.3 to 3.7$\times$ the output, depending on the per-token bound. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K context and concurrency 512, Adaptive DHiSparse with DSpark delivers 1.85$\times$ the output of resident serving with DSpark. In a load step, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows at low load and releases memory under pressure.

title: Dynamical Lie Algebras for Fixed-Gate Quantum Ansätze
abstract: Parameterized Quantum Circuits have emerged as a central framework for variational quantum algorithms in the NISQ regime, with major applications in quantum simulation, combinatorial optimization, and, more recently, quantum machine learning (QML). By developing a new approach for computing dynamical Lie algebras associated with quantum circuits combining parametrized gates and non-parametrized entangling gates, we aim to extend the applicability of recent algebraic results to architectures that are actually used in quantum machine learning.

title: OpenSocialJax: Evaluating Social Adaptation in Sequential Social Dilemmas with Open-Ended Environmental Dynamics
abstract: Sequential social dilemma benchmarks capture diverse social interactions, but rarely test whether agents can infer hidden environmental rules through repeated interaction while adapting to other agents. We introduce \textbf{OpenSocialJax}, which extends Clean Up and Commons Harvest across an open-ended distribution of latent environment configurations, systematically varying spatial layouts and hidden rules governing tool crafting, payoffs, and resource dynamics. Each episode samples one configuration from tens of millions of possibilities and holds it fixed across five trials. We evaluate eight large language models, including three closed source models and five open source models. Our evaluation tests whether models can discover hidden rules and adapt to other agents in homogeneous and mixed teams. We find that rule discovery often improves performance but does not reliably sustain cooperation, as the cleaning burden becomes concentrated among fewer agents in OpenCleanup and every team eventually exhausts the shared resource in OpenHarvest. In our mixed arena, one cooperative agent was able to sustain the public good in OpenCleanup at a cost to its own return, but could not prevent resource depletion in OpenHarvest. Together, these results highlight the difficulty of adapting jointly to unfamiliar environmental dynamics and the changing behavior of other agents.

title: Towards Understanding the Training of GFlowNets: A Theoretical Perspective
abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn policies that sample discrete objects in proportion to a positive reward. They are trained by minimizing balance objectives, whose exact satisfaction guarantees correct sampling. However, a comprehensive theory linking nonzero balance loss and approximate stationarity to sampling accuracy, especially under evolving sampling distributions and backward policies, is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we develop a unified theory for Flow Matching, Detailed Balance, and Trajectory Balance in this regime. We first bound terminal symmetric KL by the square root of the expected balance loss. Then, we show that approximate stationarity controls this distribution error up to a tangent-space residual measuring parameterization incompleteness. Finally, we establish finite-time convergence under fixed or controlled sampling and fixed, balance-trained, or separately updated backward policies. Under standard smoothness assumptions, with fixed or controlled sampling and a fixed or balance-trained backward policy, the expected loss is $O(\barε^2+T^{-1})$ and expected terminal symmetric KL is $O(\barε+T^{-1/2})$ under uniform coverage. For a separately updated backward policy, we characterize the sufficient update decay to approach the residual neighborhood and preserve these rates. These results connect balance objectives to sampling accuracy and clarify how parameterization, coverage, and moving components govern GFlowNet training.

title: Tight asymptotic competitive ratio for the Canadian Traveller Problem on unit-weighted grids
abstract: We study the $k$-Canadian Traveller Problem (k-ctp), an online navigation problem introduced by Papadimitriou and Yannakakis in 1991. Given an undirected weighted graph $G=(V,E,ω)$ and two vertices $s,t\in V$, a traveller aims at navigating from $s$ to $t$ while minimizing the total distance travelled. However, up to $k$ edges of the graph may be blocked, and the traveller discovers that an edge is blocked only upon reaching one of its endpoints. The performance of an online algorithm for k-ctp is measured with the competitive ratio, which is the quotient between the distance actually traversed and the distance traversed by an omniscient traveller who knows all blockages in advance. A general lower bound $2k+1$ for the competitive ratio of deterministic algorithms remains valid even when the input graph is series-parallel, whereas constant competitive ratios can be achieved on restricted graph classes, such as cycles or unit-weighted outerplanar graphs. In this paper, we establish the first intermediate competitive ratio between constant and linear regimes. We prove that, on unit-weighted solid grid graphs, there exists an online algorithm with competitive ratio $O(\sqrt{k})$. This ratio is asymptotically tight and cannot be defeated, even on unit-weighted square grids. Finally, we show that both the unit-weighted and solidity assumptions are essential: going further with arbitrary edge weights (even on square grids) or non-solid unit-weighted grid structures yields a linear lower bound of $Ω(k)$.

title: Relaxed Centralized Circumcentered-Reflection Methods for Convex Feasibility: Convergence and Finite Termination
abstract: Projection methods are among the most widely used techniques for solving convex feasibility problems due to their simplicity and robustness. However, classical projection-based algorithms and existing circumcentered-reflection methods generally provide only asymptotic convergence. In this paper, we introduce a relaxed version of the centralized circumcentered-reflection method (cCRM) obtained through an extrapolation of the circumcenter step. We first analyze the two-set case and then extend the proposed approach to the successive framework for multiple convex sets, including under- and over-relaxation and a backtracking strategy. The convergence analysis establishes Fejér monotonicity and global convergence under suitable conditions, while local error-bound assumptions yield linear convergence and standard regularity assumptions imply superlinear convergence. Motivated by finitely convergent projection methods based on perturbed feasible sets, we further investigate a perturbed relaxed formulation designed to achieve finite termination. Numerical experiments show good practical performance, comparable to and competitive with the finitely convergent PACA method. The results also provide clear numerical evidence of finite termination in the tested instances.

title: Dislocation mediated twin boundary faceting in $β$-Sn
abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs), including twin boundaries (TBs), play a critical role in plastic deformation by interacting with dislocations. The deformation and strengthening mechanisms in $β$-Sn are of significant interest because Sn-based alloys are widely used as solder materials. Recent experiments have shown deformation-induced faceting in $β$-Sn arising from twin-dislocation interactions. Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations informed by a recently developed machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP), we demonstrate a $\langle c\rangle$ dislocation-absorption mediated faceting reaction along $(301)$ TBs in $β$-Sn in which facet length grows with the number of absorbed dislocations. We show that the predicted facet length is consistent with isotropic elasticity theory only when the disclination character of the asymmetric twin facet is taken into account. We discuss analogies to faceting reactions in other low symmetry metals and hypothesize that the ubiquity of $(301)$ twins in $β$-Sn stems from their ability to grow rapidly through a forest of dislocation obstacles.

title: Non-Bloch band theory for finite banded non-Hermitian Toeplitz matrices
abstract: Non-Bloch band theory recovers the open-boundary spectrum of a non-Hermitian chain from its Bloch Hamiltonian evaluated along the generalised Brillouin zone rather than the unit circle. We develop its finite-size counterpart for banded Toeplitz matrices with real open-boundary spectrum. Reality of the spectrum forces the generalised Brillouin zone to be parametrised by an analytic polar curve, so the known sufficient condition for a real spectrum is also necessary under some mild non-degeneracy conditions. At finite size $n$, the eigenvalues of the original and the symmetrised Bloch Hamiltonians are given by samples at $n$ quantised momenta from the same limiting band, although separated by a phase mismatch of order $1/n$ which we obtain in closed form. Iterating this correction $K$ times yields a quantisation rule on the generalised Brillouin zone reproducing the finite spectrum with an error $\mathcal{O}(n^{-K-1})$ for any fixed $K$. At finite size, the generalised Brillouin zone itself is unchanged and only its parametrisation depends on $n$.

title: Complexity of Autobidding Equilibria in GSP Sponsored Shopping
abstract: We revisit autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions, recently proposed and studied in Dütting et al. On the existence side, we show that autobidding equilibria under both budget constraints (ABE-B) and return-on-investment constraints (ABE-R) always exist and, moreover, always admit equilibria with polynomial-size support over the allocation space. On the computational side, we show that computing an exact equilibrium is in FIXP, and that computing an approximate equilibrium is in PPAD. We also prove that computing an approximate equilibrium is PPAD-hard for both ABE-B and ABE-R. Together, these results provide a fairly comprehensive picture of the computational complexity of autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions.

title: Machine Unlearning for Federated Socially Fair k-Means Clustering
abstract: Federated clustering can support applications such as patient stratification across hospitals and customer segmentation across distributed financial datasets. Responsible AI calls for fair representation of demographic groups and support for data deletion, motivated in part by rights such as the GDPR's right to erasure. These goals interact: deleting records can change the balance between groups and alter the clustering of the remaining population. We study exact machine unlearning for federated socially fair $k$-means, whose objective is to minimize the largest group-average squared distance to the nearest center. Our approach keeps separate local summaries for each group, so summaries at unaffected institutions remain valid as global fairness weights change. For two groups, we prove an initialization approximation guarantee independent of client group proportions under ideal sampling, and we show that same-seed replay reproduces retraining exactly. Reuse pays off most when a whole client withdraws: across three datasets, replay is $35.8\times$ faster than retraining for the initialization-only model and remains $2.4\times$ and $1.7\times$ faster with one and two fair-refinement rounds, which improve worst-group cost. For individual record deletions, gains are modest (about $1.06\times$), and certifying cached assignments can cost more than it saves. These results map where exact unlearning can profitably reuse computation. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/arareddy/mufsc.

title: Holomorphic approximation for Hamiltonian diffeomorphism groups via the Symplectic Density Property
abstract: We show that the cotangent bundle of a holomorphically flexible Stein manifold has the symplectic density property. As application we deduce holomorphic approximation for Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms of real cotangent bundles by complex symplectic automorphisms of the complexified cotangent bundles, which preserve the real bundle, in the Carleman sense, i.e. in the Whitney topology.

title: High Resolution Spectro-Polarimetric Observations of the Optical Filaments surrounding NGC 1275 with ESPaDOnS
abstract: We analyze archival high spectral resolution ESPaDOnS spectropolarimetric observations (R = $λ/Δλ$ = 68000) of three targeted locations within the filamentary nebula surrounding NGC 1275. We present here the analysis of the main filaments emission lines, namely: [NII]$\lambda6584$, H$α$, and [NII]$\lambda6548$, across our three pointings displaying clear detectable emission, with one also showing additional [SII]$\lambda6716$ and [SII]$\lambda6731$ emission line doublet. Using a Markov Chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) algorithm and thanks to the exceptionally high spectral resolution of the observations, we resolve for the first time each of the emission lines within one of the pointings into a set of three emission components with a remarkable velocity dispersion contrast ($σ_1 \sim 25$ km/s, $σ_2 \sim 90$ km/s and $σ_3 \sim 208$ km/s). We also perform flux ratios of the three detected emission components, which reveal differences in electron density and ionization sources. Consequently, the ESPaDOnS observations appear to reveal for the first time the overlap of an outer quiescent filament and a central turbulent filament likely affected by the AGN activity at a distance of $\sim 6.8''$ ($\sim 2.5$ kpc) from the central BCG. Finally, ESPaDOnS polarimetric data of one of the pointing allows us to confirm an average linear polarization degree of $\sim 0.15-0.14\%$ and an angle of polarization of $5.3\pm25.7^\circ$ for the optical emission of the filaments, as well as polarization dips associated with the H$α$ emission line and its multiple emission components. We interpret these features and measurements as tentative polarization due to dust scattering.

title: State-Isolated Vision Mamba via Update-Tendency Routing for Underwater Image Enhancement
abstract: Vision Mamba has recently emerged as an efficient alternative to convolutional and Transformer-based architectures by modeling long-range spatial dependencies through recurrent state evolution. Existing studies primarily improve token serialization, scanning strategies, or expert routing, yet largely overlook a state level question question: how should recurrent states be organized for spatially heterogeneous visual restoration? In this paper, we show that forcing tokens with heterogeneous update behaviors to recurrently modify a shared hidden state leads to persistent cross-content interference, which we term \textbf{State Contention}. We further argue that effective recurrent modeling should organize state evolution according to token compatibility rather than token ordering. Based on this observation, we introduce \textbf{State Isolation}, a new recurrent state organization principle for Vision Mamba,tokens with compatible state-update tendencies evolve within independent recurrent state streams. To instantiate this principle, we propose \textbf{IsoMamba}, a $Δ$-guided architecture that constructs model-intrinsic update representations, discovers update-compatible token groups through label-free clustering, and routes them to isolated Mamba experts following a \textbf{cluster--route--isolate} paradigm. In addition, we develop a dynamic channel-wise reweighting objective to compensate for wavelength-dependent reconstruction difficulty in underwater images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IsoMamba consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple underwater image enhancement benchmarks while providing cleaner hidden state responses, validating the effectiveness of state isolated recurrent modeling.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Systems Biology Reconstruction of Diabetic Bone Marrow Dysfunction
abstract: This study aimed to reconstruct a regulatory network suitable for systems biology analysis of diabetic bone marrow. Three artificial intelligence large language models independently analysed 18 Discovery and 43 Validation publications. Investigator guided integration produced a frozen network of 62 biological entities and 79 directed interactions. Open source software Gephi created a visual representation before and after main node removal. The plausibility of the reconstructed interactions was tested against independent curated knowledge resources, including the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, connectomeDB2025, Reactome, and Gene Ontology. Further analysis examined physiological correspondence, missing edge sensitivity, and graph constrained interrogation. Functional modules encompassed endothelial perivascular support, stem cell retention and trafficking, neural circadian regulation, inflammatory myelopoiesis, metabolic stress, and epigenetic regulation. They intersected through shared effects on endothelial function and stem cell behaviour. The endothelium was the principal connecting node. Computational removal of the endothelial node increased network fragmentation and diameter, while average directed path length remained essentially unchanged. External resources supported 60/79 interactions (75.9%); 19 remained unresolved, with none classified as contradictory. Complementary assessments supported biological plausibility and faithful interrogation of the reconstructed network. This investigator led dialogue with artificial intelligence provides a foundation for a systems level understanding of diabetic bone marrow dysfunction. The approach may facilitate the generation of testable hypotheses and the identification of mechanistic targets for coordinated restoration of disrupted niche interactions.

title: Enhancing Legal Reasoning in Pre-trained Language Models via Knowledge Graph-Guided Multi-Task Pre-training
abstract: Legal language understanding requires reasoning over semi-structured regulatory documents, yet standard pre-training objectives do not explicitly target this structural capability. Because current legal language models rely solely on masked language modeling, they treat statutory text as flat token sequences and ignore the underlying hierarchical constraints. To bridge this gap, we present a multi-task pre-training approach for German traffic law (StVO). Our approach combines three complementary objectives: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP), Knowledge Graph (KG) Guided Clustering (CLU), and Knowledge Graph (KG) Aware Paragraph Classification (CLS). This approach explicitly encodes structured legal knowledge directly into the model weights. This encoding enables zero-shot legal reasoning at inference time and removes the need for discrete graph traversal. We evaluate our approach across nine Transformer-based encoders and 324 experimental runs. On synthetic StVO question answering, our models demonstrate consistent relative improvements between 10.3% and 155.0% over baselines. Furthermore, relative to the established LexGLUE baselines (Chalkidis et al., 2022), our models improve over prior results on four of seven legal benchmarks. It also achieves consistent zero-shot transfer gains between 3.4% and 15.8% on Austrian driving regulations. These experimental results indicate that our training approach generalizes successfully beyond the initial training legal domain.

title: List chromatic number of $G(n,r,s)$ graphs
abstract: We study the list chromatic number of generalized Johnson graphs. Recall that the vertices of such graphs are all possible $r$-element subsets of $[n] = \{1, \dotsc, n\}$ and an edge is drawn between two vertices if and only if corresponding sets have exactly $s$ common elements. We prove that for any fixed $s \geq 1$ and $r \geq 2s + 2$ we have $χ_L(G(n,r,s)) = Θ(n^{s+1}\ln n)$. In case where $s = 0$ we prove that for all $4\ln n \leq r \leq n/20$ we have $χ_L(G(n,r,0)) \geq \frac{n}{120}\ln\left\{\frac{en}{r}\right\}$. Together with previous results of Bulankina, Inozemtsev and Kupavskii this proves that $χ_L(G(n,r,0)) = Θ\left\{n\ln\left\{\frac{en}{r}\right\}\right\}$ uniformly for $2 \leq r \leq (1/2-\varepsilon)n$.

title: Amortized Counterfactual Prediction with Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Counterfactual inference asks how an observed outcome might have differed under different circumstances, such as whether a patient would have recovered had they received a different treatment. Such questions arise whenever decisions depend on the outcomes of alternatives that were not observed. Answering counterfactual queries generally requires knowledge of the underlying causal structure, which is often unavailable in practice. A common approach is therefore to first estimate the causal graph from observational data and then perform counterfactual inference. However, errors in the estimated causal graph can propagate to downstream counterfactual predictions. To address this challenge, we introduce the Counterfactual Graph Neural Process (CFGNP), an end-to-end approach that answers counterfactual queries directly from observational data without first estimating a causal graph. CFGNP uses Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to exploit the dual-graph structure by restricting cross-world message passing to corresponding factual--counterfactual variables. Across synthetic and image-based benchmarks, CFGNP achieves stronger predictive performance than existing approaches, including on the German Loan benchmark, where it reduces MSE from $4.51 \times 10^{-2}$ to $0.19 \times 10^{-2}$. Furthermore, on synthetic causal graphs, a model trained only on 10-node graphs maintains strong predictive performance on graphs with up to 30 nodes, without retraining.

title: The Distortion of Threshold Approval Multiwinner Voting
abstract: We study multiwinner voting with $n$ voters and $m$ candidates, where the goal is to select a committee of size $k$. Voters have unit-sum cardinal utilities but report only coarse information induced by $t$ utility thresholds. In particular, each voter partitions the candidates into approval sets, with the utilities of all candidates in the same set lying between the same pair of consecutive thresholds. We model the utility of each voter for a committee as a normalized monotone symmetric norm, capturing, among others, additive welfare, best-representative utility, top-$r$ welfare, $\ell_p$ welfare, and normalized non-increasing ordered weighted averages. We design a deterministic rule with distortion at most $2(2m)^{1/t}$ and a randomized rule with distortion at most $2\min\{m^{1/(t+1)},m/k\}$. These guarantees hold for every committee size $k$ and every norm in our framework. Consequently, a single threshold yields distortion $O(m)$ for deterministic rules and $O(\sqrt{m})$ for randomized rules, while $O(\log m)$ thresholds suffice for constant distortion. We complement these results with norm-dependent lower bounds that asymptotically match our upper bounds for constant committee sizes, including the single-winner case.

title: Turbulence modes in molecular clouds in M33: a challenging test of the Brunt-Federrath framework
abstract: Understanding the turbulent structure of molecular clouds is essential for linking galactic environment to the regulation of star formation. Although Galactic molecular clouds have been studied extensively, extending turbulence-mode analysis beyond the Milky Way remains challenging because of the limited spatial resolution and dynamic range of extragalactic observations. We assess the applicability of the Brunt \& Federrath (2014; BF14) framework to molecular clouds in M33. We apply BF14 to 128 $^{13}$CO(2-1) clouds, selecting a primary quality-controlled sample of 54 clouds and a more restrictive 25-cloud subsample defined using a stricter extraction-padding criterion (PAD=2) for quantitative analysis.Tests of cloud and noise power spectra, Fourier-space cutoffs, extraction padding, and Monte Carlo uncertainties demonstrate that the retained spatial frequencies are dominated by astrophysical signal and that the inferred turbulence-mode fractions are robust against reasonable analysis choices. Both samples yield consistent distributions of the solenoidal fraction, with mean values of $R \simeq 0.22$ for both samples and median values of $R \simeq 0.18$ and $0.17$, respectively, indicating that compressive motions dominate the turbulent energy budget. No strong systematic variations of $R$ are found with galactocentric distance or tracers of recent star formation. These results demonstrate that, despite the challenging spatial resolution of current extragalactic molecular-line observations, the BF14 framework can be applied reliably to nearby galaxies using spectroscopic observations alone. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first application of the full BF14 formalism to extragalactic molecular-cloud observations.

title: Anomaly induced transport in holographic superconductors
abstract: We investigate the anomaly-induced transport properties of a holographic superconductor exhibiting spontaneous symmetry breaking. The holographic model incorporates vector and axial gauge fields, an additional non-anomalous $U(1)$ symmetry, and a charged scalar field that drives the phase transition. Working in the probe limit, we numerically construct the superconducting background under two alternative scalar field quantizations, corresponding to operators with scaling dimensions $Δ=1$ and $Δ=3$ (denoted as the $O_1$ and $O_2$ theories, respectively). Using Kubo formulae, we compute the chiral magnetic conductivities and examine their response to the scalar condensate. Our findings demonstrate that spontaneous symmetry breaking allows anomaly-induced transport to extend beyond anomalous currents, significantly impacting the non-anomalous sector as well. Remarkably, this effect appears in both theories, indicating that the influence on the non-anomalous sector is independent of the chosen quantization. The comparison of our numerical results with the analytical limits for $O_i \to 0$ and $O_i \to \infty$ $(i=1,2)$ reveals consistent behavior across both theories.

title: Chiroptical Nonlinearity Found in Covalent Organic Frameworks
abstract: Chiroptical nonlinearity is vital for modern optics and photonics. However, it remains a central challenge to obtain a material simultaneously with large second-order nonlinearity and strong nonlinear optical chirality. Here we uncover the strong chiroptical nonlinearity in COF-330-a, owing to the formation of unique chiral, polar structure with large p-electron conjugation via structural transformation. A large effective second-order nonlinear susceptibility of ~ 101 pm/V and a strong nonlinear chiroptical response (SHG-CD: -1.60 to +1.66) have been demonstrated in individual COF-330-a microcrystals, transcending the performance trade-off limitation in conventional chiroptical materials. These findings open a new avenue for designing nonlinear chiroptical crystals which harness the duality of polarity and chirality and chemical versatility of COFs.

title: Shear-driven arrest of dip-coating film entrainment
abstract: A plate withdrawn from a bath of partially wetting liquid entrains a film above a critical velocity. Here, we show that this critical threshold can be substantially increased by the presence of a laminar gas flow opposed to the plate velocity that exerts a tangential shear stress on the liquid-gas interface. Using two-phase immiscible Navier-Stokes simulations and confining the gas to a narrow channel, we derive a closed-form expression for the interfacial stress, which combined with lubrication theory relates the thickness of the film and the contact line velocity to the applied shear stress. As the gas velocity is increased, the film thins and the contact line velocity slows down, until the imposed shear overcomes the drag of the moving plate and entrainment is arrested. As in the quiescent case, the velocity mismatch between plate and contact line is independent of the plate velocity and is set by the applied shear alone. We find that one set of varying gas flow simulations, with constant critical plate velocity, therefore determines the critical gas flow for every smaller plate velocity.

title: SeoulMMOD: A Large-Scale Multimodal Origin-Destination Flow Benchmark
abstract: Origin-destination (OD) flow forecasting supports urban mobility decisions by predicting the volume and patterns of human movement across a city. Most existing public OD benchmarks provide only a partial view of citywide mobility, covering a single transport service or at most two modes. With partial mode coverage, observed demand changes are difficult to separate into shifts across transport modes and changes in total travel. We introduce SeoulMMOD, a large-scale public benchmark for citywide multimodal mobility in Seoul. SeoulMMOD provides three years of hourly OD flows estimating total mobility for 6 urban travel modes across 25 districts and 426 sub-districts, together with travel-time, travel-distance, calendar, rainfall, and point-of-interest (POI) signals. Using SeoulMMOD, we benchmark 14 forecasting baselines under a common protocol and analyse the effects of spatial scaling, joint versus mode-separate training, and cross-year generalization. Results show that several spatio-temporal models that work at district level do not scale to sub-district OD forecasting, and that naive joint multi-mode training does not consistently improve accuracy. Together, the dataset and benchmark establish a reproducible testbed for multi-mode, multi-year OD forecasting at the city scale.

title: confoundvis for Visualizing and Reporting Sensitivity to Unmeasured Confounding in R
abstract: Sensitivity analysis asks how strong unmeasured confounding would have to be before an observational conclusion changes. Established methods answer this question using different quantities, including partial $R^2$ values, correlation products, and risk ratios. In this article, we present confoundvis, an R package that organizes these results through a common object, plotting functions, and reports. It calculates partial $R^2$ and impact-threshold paths from fitted linear models, imports results from sensemakr, konfound, and EValue, and provides measured-covariate benchmarks for the OLS frameworks. We demonstrate the workflow with 5,735 patients from the right heart catheterization study. The adjusted linear probability coefficient is 0.0634, the point-null robustness value is 0.0608, and the conditional significance impact threshold is 0.0376. The largest adverse leave-one-term-out measured-covariate product is 0.0090. Because the benchmark and threshold use different conditioning sets, their ratio is descriptive. A separate modified Poisson model gives a risk ratio of 1.103 and an E-value of 1.439. The contribution is a software workflow that keeps each method's units and decision rule clear. The package is available from CRAN.

title: LAPT-Scale: Scaling Embodied Policies with Latent Action Pre-Training on Human Videos
abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions.

title: KVeil: First-Place Solution to ECCV 2026 LifeGenIP Challenge on Unlearnable Videos
abstract: The rapid development of personalized video generation has raised serious concerns over identity privacy, as a few facial videos of a person now suffice to reproduce their identity in synthetic videos. This report presents the first-place solutions to both phases of the ECCV 2026 LifeGenIP Challenge on Unlearnable Videos, which aims to protect facial videos from unauthorized customization under a limited and imperceptible perturbation budget. For Phase 1, we introduce Reference Capacity Collapse, a pair of complementary losses that degrade the information carried by the reference condition while keeping subsequent video representations dependent on it, together with a Motion-Guided EOT mechanism that improves robustness across unknown inference conditions. Phase 2 further considers tuning-based customization and unseen generative models. To address both threats within a single perturbation, we design a two-layer framework that protects the facial and background regions separately, constructing structure-aligned perturbations from a synthetic target identity in the former and strengthening the white-box disruption of Phase 1 in the latter. Our method achieves nearly perfect protection under white-box reference-based customization, and remains effective under other customization paradigms, various models, and temporal attacks. Both solutions are built upon our recent work LETHE. We hope our solutions can inspire future work on protecting facial videos against unauthorized customization. Our code is available at https://github.com/AntigoneRandy/KVeil.

title: The tensor product of the Fremlin tensor product of Banach lattice algebras
abstract: We study the Arens regularity of the Fremlin projective tensor product of Banach lattice algebras. We firrst introduce and investigate L-weakly almost periodic functionals, a class of functionals defind in terms of L-weak compactness of their orbits. We obtain a characterization of these functionals in terms of bounded disjoint sequences and use it to analyze the Fremlin projective tensor product. In particular, we prove that, for nontrivial Banach attice algebras A and B, Arens regularity of A j jB implies Arens regularity of both A and B. The converse, however, fails: we construct two Arens regular Banach lattice algebras whose Fremlin projective tensor product is not Arens regular. We also establish several sufficient conditions for the Arens regularity of A j jB, including conditions involving the positive Schur property and order continuity of the norm on the space of regular operators. Finally, we show that when both factors are Banach f-algebras, their Fremlin projective tensor product is Arens regular.

title: Orthros: Phase-Aware Heterogeneous Attention for Efficient Transformers
abstract: Efficient attention mechanisms, such as linear and sliding window attention, aim to reduce the computational complexity of Transformers from quadratic to linear. However, their degraded in-context recall often necessitates interleaving full attention layers, leaving the quadratic bottleneck unresolved in long-context processing. To address this, we introduce Orthros attention, which shifts the efficiency paradigm from structural allocation to phase-aware decoupling. As a unified module, it dynamically switches its computation pattern across different phases of sequence processing, enabling linear complexity prefilling and full attention decoding. Our design grants Orthros attention a lower asymptotic complexity compared to vanilla Transformers in prevalent long-context scenarios characterized by heavy prefilling and light decoding. Beyond theoretical formulation and complexity analysis, extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate Orthros's superiority across multiple dimensions. First, we validate its fundamental language modeling capabilities, demonstrating scalability across varying model sizes and strong competitiveness in comprehensive architectural comparisons. Second, Orthros exhibits exceptional conversion feasibility via a data-efficient Transformer-to-Orthros conversion, yielding performance that even surpasses the original Transformer. Finally, Orthros achieves a $21.9\times$ prefilling speedup over Transformers with end-to-end inference gains, while preserving long-context capabilities, as demonstrated by near-perfect 128K needle-in-a-haystack results and Transformer-level performance on real-world in-context recall tasks. Overall, these advantages in high performance, flexibility, and efficiency position Orthros as a promising candidate to succeed the Transformer in industrial applications.

title: Adjoint-Based Stochastic Analysis for Fatigue of Aeroelastic and Frictional Systems
abstract: As engineering systems are optimized to reduce weight and improve performance, vibration behavior, including nonlinear effects, is becoming increasingly important to analyze. While methods such as harmonic balance are popular for analyzing periodic nonlinear vibration behavior, these analyses often only consider deterministic loading. However, real applications experience additional noise in the excitation, and alternative approaches are frequently limited to smaller models. This work expands on a recent approach to calculate a time-varying covariance using a linearized system around a periodic nonlinear response. Specifically, numerical conditioning is addressed and improved for cases increasing from a few degrees of freedom to hundreds of degrees of freedom. The algorithm is then extended to capture correlations across both space and time via a period-spanning covariance matrix. Model reduction is proposed for this calculation to maintain computational efficiency. The period-spanning covariance matrix is used to sample full stochastic cycles and estimate fatigue-relevant statistics up to 1393 times faster than stochastic time integration. Importantly, the present methodology uses the same gradient information as stability analyses and continuation solutions, so it can easily be applied for many nonlinear analyses. The methodology is demonstrated for two beam systems: one with unsteady aerodynamic forces and another with a Bouc-Wen frictional tip force. For the aeroelastic model, statistics are accurately estimated via the present approach. For the frictional system, some errors are introduced compared to stochastic time integration and are attributed to the linear time-periodic nature of the system used in the present stochastic calculations. However, estimated stochastic statistics remain useful given the significant reduction in computation time.

title: SafeDiSTL: Decomposing Joint Constraints for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent tasks often impose constraints on a shared objective or collective safety. A team level violation cost function can measure this constraint outcome, but does not distinguish which agents' actions most strongly influence that violation. We present SafeDiSTL, a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that allows for credit assignment even with joint constraint measurements. We use Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to measure episode-level violation through running-maximum cost increments. Smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable dynamics provide action sensitivities, which allocate each cost increment across agents at the same decision time. These sensitivities account for delayed effects when weighting agents' shares of each cost increment. We study the framework in cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control tasks. SafeDiSTL achieves 1.6-5.1x the safe-success rate in transport, improves navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivers 50-68% more throughput in traffic when compared to constrained baselines. Results demonstrate a strong improvement of the learned policy in dealing with shared constraint while retaining the performance of unconstrained policies.

title: Sharp upper bounds for Steklov eigenvalues on warped products
abstract: We obtain sharp isoperimetric-type upper bounds for Steklov eigenvalues on warped products whose bases are compact Riemannian manifolds with boundary and whose fibres are closed Riemannian manifolds. These bounds involve the volume of the warped product and of its boundary, as well as the eigenvalues of the Laplace operator on the fibre and the Steklov eigenvalues of the base. After separation of variables, these bounds are obtained by comparison with auxiliary Helmholtz-Steklov problems on the base involving weighted Laplace operators naturally induced by the warping function. We also study the effect of various natural geometric constraints, such as the warping function being identically equal to one on the boundary. The proofs make use of various spectral approximation methods, including homogenisation on manifolds when the fibres are one-dimensional.

title: Relaxation Dark Energy: Compositional Dynamics and the Future of Cosmic Acceleration
abstract: If cosmic acceleration is driven by a positive cosmological constant, the universe approaches an eternally accelerating de Sitter state, whose interpretation in quantum gravity remains elusive. We develop a framework in which acceleration is instead a transient stage of dark-sector relaxation towards compositional equilibrium: matter and dark energy approach a stationary density ratio, eventually diluting like pressureless matter. Guided by linear response theory and Onsager's near-equilibrium regression hypothesis, we describe this evolution through a composition variable measuring departure from equilibrium. Extending constant fractional relaxation to the full background evolution yields the dark-energy equation of state $w=w_0a^{-n}$, where $n$ is the relaxation rate per e-fold of expansion. This history connects early dark-energy suppression, an upward phantom crossing and a density maximum to a pressureless scaling future. Using DESI DR2 BAO and Planck distance priors, with and without three alternative supernova compilations, we find a nominal $2.6$--$3.6σ$ preference for nonzero relaxation over constant $w$. The composition framework also motivates a constitutive prescription for linear perturbations that remains regular at phantom crossing. Near equilibrium, regular long-wavelength composition disturbances relax at the background rate to leading order, while small-scale fluctuations propagate as damped sound waves. We prove, however, that for separately conserved matter and dark energy, the pointwise constitutive relation cannot sustain a regular, gradient-stable negative-pressure branch throughout its full past evolution. We explore modifications of the pressure response and their consistency with neighbouring homogeneous histories, identifying requirements for extending the near-equilibrium description to the full cosmological evolution.

title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.

title: Stabilized SQP Method for Convex Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Composite Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper addresses the local convergence analysis of the stabilized sequential quadratic programming method for a class of composite optimization problems with convex piecewise linear- quadratic (CPLQ) modeling functions. We demonstrate that an appropriate second-order sufficient condition (SOSC) -formulated for composite problems- alone is sufficient to guarantee local superlin- ear convergence of the primal-dual sequence generated by this method. Furthermore, we examine the relaxation of the SOSC and show that it can be replaced with a weaker noncriticality of the associated Lagrange multiplier, provided, the modeling function is polyhedral and a relative interior condition is satisfied. We also present counterexamples showing that the relative interior condition is indispensable and that this relaxation fails for general CPLQ modeling functions.

title: A strategy for astrometric quasar selection with Gaia DR3 and its application to discover new luminous $z>2$ quasars
abstract: We aim to provide a cookbook for purely astrometric selection of quasars with Gaia DR3 and to provide an example of its use for the identification of very luminous $z>2$ quasars. We analyse the Gaia DR3 astrometry of confirmed quasars and stationary sources. We show that the proper motion signal to noise $μ/σ_μ$ follows a Rayleigh-like distribution. We also show the importance of properly taking into account the correlation between proper motions in right ascension and declination, as well as the non-linear error propagation. We adopt the Mahalanobis distance to the null proper-motion hypothesis. A scaled $χ^2$ distribution with $k=2$ and scale $s=1.1485$ is fitted to Gaia-CRF3; the corresponding $\pm2σ$ Gaussian-equivalent threshold is $D^2_{M(μ)}<7.097$. The final criteria combine this with the parallax condition and $\mathrm{ruwe}<1.4$. Applying the new criteria to the SDSS DR16Q confirmed quasars, the recovery rate is $90.25\%$. The suggested purely astrometric selection significantly improves both completeness and purity compared to other strategies used in the literature, reaching a quasar purity of approximately $95\%$ ($\sim2σ$ Gaussian-equivalent). It can be used to improve the selection purity and completeness for future quasar surveys. As an example, we use the suggested strategi to locate 24 very bright $z>2$ quasars without redshifts in the literature. Our proposed astrometric selection strategy recovers 95\% of known quasars. Its potential use for new discoveries is demonstrated by the identification of 24 very luminous $z>2$ quasars. Ten of these are new discoveries and for an additional seven we correct the redshifts determined by other methods.}

title: Perturbed isotropic oscillators with inversion symmetry
abstract: We consider the normal form of a 1:1 detuned resonance that can be related, via a double averaging process, to the three body problem of celestial mechanics. In view of the symmetry in the gravitational coupling between the planets, the obtained normal form exhibits inversion symmetry. We provide an analytical prediction of the possible bifurcations in terms of the detunings and the other physical parameters of the system. We show that the bifurcation scenario is rich. It includes bifurcation sequences where the unstable orbit appearing after a saddle-node bifurcation can have a reversed pitchfork bifurcation, where it turns into stability with the birth of two unstable orbits, which eventually reconnect with one of the two quasi-normal modes. Furthermore, another scenario shows a standard pitchfork in which one of the quasi-normal modes becomes unstable, giving rise to a pair of stable periodic orbits. By introducing coupling and asymmetry parameters, we provide an effective way to discern all the possible sequences of bifurcations.

title: A Privileged Teacher That Only Scores Cannot Search: Critique-Conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning
abstract: On-policy self-distillation promises to replace the sparse outcome signal of verifiable-reward RL with dense token-level credit: a teacher conditioned on the reference solution scores the student's own rollout, and the resulting distributional shift is distilled back into the policy. We investigate whether this scoring signal actually contains corrective credit. Using gold error spans in student rollouts, we test the two signals consumed by self-distillation objectives, the full-distribution KL and the token log-ratio, for two properties: whether they localize errors and whether they push probability away from erroneous student tokens. They exhibit neither of these properties nor can they reliably distinguish correct from incorrect rollouts within the same problem. We argue that this failure is structural: locating an error in a reasoning trace is itself a search problem, while a scoring teacher is never explicitly asked to perform that search. The same model, with the same privileged information, localizes errors substantially better when allowed to generate a critique. This forms the motivation for \emph{critique-conditioned self-distillation}: first generate a critique of the current rollout, then condition the scoring teacher on that critique. The resulting signal localizes errors, is corrective within error spans, and shifts probability toward tokens that initiate backtracking such as ``Wait'', ``But'', and ``Actually''. We further show that the critique is useful both at test time, where resuming a wrong rollout with the critique in context converts math problems the model cannot solve by sampling, and in cold-start GRPO, where it provides an advantage signal on prompts for which verifiable rewards alone provide none.

title: The $E_6$ normal forms: semisimple deformations, geometry, DT invariants, and the $E_{6,\infty}$ order
abstract: We study the completed Jacobi algebras of $x^3+xy^3+p(y)$ for $\operatorname{ord}_yp=n\ge4$. The explicit normal-form morsification, the filtered length and centre proofs, and the cyclic terminal identities give finite free semisimple deformations. For every parameter of finite order we construct a polynomial curve neighbourhood and a local projective small contraction; the resulting geometric GV and Donaldson--Thomas calculations identify the block multiplicities. The one-dimensional limit $E_{6,\infty}$ is studied separately as an order: we determine its normalization, conductor, radical-idealizer chain, and maximal overorders. The canonical chain yields a nine-dimensional finite quotient whose Ringel dual is isomorphic to its opposite. An expanded construction gives a choice-independent $22$-dimensional quotient and a $40$-dimensional Ringel dual; a corner quotient relates the two finite constructions. The length and centre formulas are proved by a filtered comparison with a homogeneous matrix order and by terminal identities at the exceptional endpoint.

title: Topping's conjecture for solutions of harmonic map flow with isolated bubbles
abstract: By establishing a weighted Lojasiewicz-Simon inequality for maps which are close to a fixed harmonic map modulo scaling, we prove Topping's conjecture on continuity of the body map in the case of finite time singularities at which only isolated bubbles form.

title: Travel time tomography for elliptically anisotropic elastic planar media
abstract: We study the gauge of the travel time tomography problem for elliptically anisotropic planar media. Under this assumption the respective slowness surfaces consist of an inner ellipse and an outer circle. Hence, the singularities of seismic waves propagate on geodesics given by two Riemannian metrics of which the one related to shear waves is conformally Euclidean. We show that if both of these metrics are lens rigid then, up to boundary fixing diffeomorphisms, each elliptically anisotropic stiffness tensor is uniquely determined by the lens data whenever it has at least one isotropic point. If none of those points exists, then there are exactly two elliptically anisotropic stiffness tensors with the same lens data. Clearly, not all boundary fixing diffeomorphisms preserve the imposed structure of the slowness surface. We show that the set of well-behaved diffeomorphisms is never a subgroup of all boundary fixing diffeomorphisms. Our proofs are based on an interplay of algebra and geometry, and the key of the proofs is a characterization of the elliptic anisotropy via several polynomial conditions.

title: Arrested phase separation and amorphous patterns in charged binary fluids
abstract: Frustration generated by competing interactions can stabilise patterns with tunable lengthscales which evade indefinite coarsening and macroscopic phase separation. Here we investigate a charged binary fluid in which the tendency toward phase separation is opposed by screened electrostatic repulsion. Combining analytics and numerical simulations, we identify a regime of arrested phase separation characterised by finite-wavelength instability. The resulting states include droplet and labyrinthine phases in two dimensions, and droplets, concentric shells and tubular structures in three dimensions. Surprisingly, some of these structures are amorphous morphologies that emerge reproducibly from different initial conditions. Free-energy estimates suggest that these disordered structures may be thermodynamically stabilised by frustration, rather than being kinetically trapped. Our results identify a simple mechanism through which the competition between phase separation and screened electrostatics can generate equilibrium amorphous microphases with glassy features.

title: RAPID: Proactive Rate Control for Enabling High Data Rate and Low Latency in 5G Edge Networks
abstract: Many 6G use cases such as tactile Internet and eXtended reality applications would simultaneously require a high data rate and low latency wireless connectivity.It is increasingly being realized that the current transport protocols relying on packet loss and delay are insufficient to satisfy the data rate and latency requirements of such applications. To address this problem, we propose RAPID, a transport layer solution designed for private 5G edge networks, where the bottleneck is located at the base station. We show that by regulating the send rate to maintain a target physical resource block utilization, we can achieve high data rate, low latency communication. We design a simple yet effective policy that adapts to the dynamic nature of wireless channel conditions. In a multi-UE scenario with two RAPID flows and one TCP Cubic flow, our testbed results show that RAPID flows achieve significant improvements in one-way delay, i.e., 72x and 55x lower compared to TCP Cubic, with negligible packet loss at the cost of modest goodput reductions of 16% and 27%, respectively.

title: Studying the Effects of Task Diversity Using Small Mathematical Worlds
abstract: Basic mathematical tasks like modular addition have been a valuable tool for illuminating aspects of neural network behavior that are challenging to see in noisy, unverifiable, large-scale, real-world settings. These studies have typically focused on a single task. However, modern language models are exposed to a vast number of tasks despite being trained with a next-token prediction objective. In this work, we introduce two mathematical task ecosystems, IntWorld and PermWorld, built from distinct but related tasks on integers and permutations. Both are designed to simulate task diversity within a cohesive mathematical 'world' where tasks are distinct but related.
